courses.title: Internal Medicine II: Endocrinology, Nephrology and Gastroenterology
courses.description: Diabetes mellitus and its complications, thyroid and adrenal disease, kidney disease, liver disease and gastrointestinal disorders.

topics.title: Diabetes Mellitus
topics.summary: Diagnosis, types, management, and chronic complications.

material.heading: Diagnosis and treatment
material.body: Diabetes mellitus affects about 3–6% of Nigerian adults, with many undiagnosed. Diagnostic criteria: fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), 2-hour glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L on OGTT, HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), or random glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss). Type 1 (autoimmune β-cell destruction, insulin-dependent, ketosis-prone) and type 2 (insulin resistance with relative deficiency — about 90%); ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes ('Flatbush') is recognised in Africans. Management of type 2: education, diet and exercise, metformin first-line (avoid if eGFR < 30; GI effects, lactic acidosis rarely), then sulfonylureas (hypoglycaemia risk — glibenclamide common in Nigeria), DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists (cardiorenal benefits), and insulin. Targets: HbA1c about 7% (individualised), BP < 130/80, statins for most adults over 40. Hypoglycaemia (glucose < 4 mmol/L): conscious — oral glucose; unconscious — IV 50% (or 10%) dextrose or IM glucagon.

material.heading: Complications
material.body: Acute: diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA — glucose > 11 mmol/L, ketones, acidosis pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15; precipitated by infection or missed insulin; treat with IV fluids (0.9% saline), fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h, potassium replacement and treat the cause) and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS — older type 2 patients, very high glucose > 30 mmol/L, osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg, marked dehydration, little ketosis; cautious fluid replacement). Chronic microvascular: retinopathy (annual fundoscopy), nephropathy (albuminuria — ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i), neuropathy (peripheral sensory loss — foot ulcers). Macrovascular: coronary disease, stroke and peripheral arterial disease. Diabetic foot disease is a major cause of amputation in Nigeria — daily foot inspection, proper footwear, avoid walking barefoot and traditional remedies, and early treatment of ulcers and infection. Screening for complications should be regular.

topics.title: Thyroid, Adrenal and Pituitary Disorders
topics.summary: Thyrotoxicosis, hypothyroidism, goitre, Addison's disease, Cushing's syndrome and pituitary disease.

material.heading: Thyroid
material.body: Goitre is common in iodine-deficient areas (historically endemic in parts of Nigeria; universal salt iodisation has reduced it). Thyrotoxicosis: weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations (sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation), anxiety, diarrhoea, and eye signs; causes — Graves' disease (commonest; diffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema; TSH-receptor antibodies), toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma, thyroiditis. Tests: suppressed TSH with raised free T4/T3. Treatment: beta-blockers for symptoms, carbimazole or propylthiouracil (agranulocytosis — warn to report sore throat; PTU preferred in first trimester), radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy (complications: recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, hypocalcaemia). Thyroid storm is an emergency. Hypothyroidism: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes; raised TSH with low free T4 (primary — Hashimoto's, post-treatment); treat with levothyroxine.

material.heading: Adrenal and pituitary
material.body: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency — autoimmune, TB (important in Nigeria), HIV-related, adrenal haemorrhage): fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyperpigmentation (skin creases, buccal mucosa), hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia; confirmed by short Synacthen test; treat with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, with sick-day rules. Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and saline. Cushing's syndrome (glucocorticoid excess — commonly iatrogenic, including skin-lightening creams with potent steroids used in Nigeria; pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease), adrenal tumours, ectopic ACTH): central obesity, moon face, purple striae, proximal myopathy, hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis; screen with overnight dexamethasone suppression test or 24-hour urinary cortisol. Pituitary tumours cause mass effects (bitemporal hemianopia) and hormone excess — prolactinoma (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea — dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine), acromegaly (GH — IGF-1, OGTT suppression test) — or hypopituitarism (e.g. Sheehan's syndrome after postpartum haemorrhage).
keyPoints: Addison's: hyperpigmentation, low Na, high K

topics.title: Kidney Disease
topics.summary: Acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, glomerular disease and renal replacement therapy.

material.heading: AKI and glomerular disease
material.body: Acute kidney injury (KDIGO: creatinine rise ≥ 26.5 µmol/L in 48 h, ≥ 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h) is classified as pre-renal (hypovolaemia — diarrhoea, haemorrhage; sepsis), intrinsic (acute tubular necrosis, nephrotoxins — aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast, herbal remedies; glomerulonephritis; malaria — blackwater fever) and post-renal (obstruction — BPH, stones, cervical cancer). Management: fluids for hypovolaemia, stop nephrotoxins, treat cause, and manage complications — hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate to protect the heart, insulin–dextrose, salbutamol, then remove potassium), fluid overload, acidosis and uraemia; indications for dialysis: refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload, uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy), and certain poisonings. Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria > 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia (causes include minimal change disease, FSGS — HIV-associated nephropathy, membranous — hepatitis B, malaria P. malariae). Nephritic syndrome: haematuria, hypertension, oliguria and oedema (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

material.heading: Chronic kidney disease
material.body: CKD is kidney damage or eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for > 3 months, staged G1–G5 and by albuminuria (A1–A3). In Nigeria, leading causes are hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, diabetes, HIV and obstructive uropathy; patients often present late with end-stage disease. People of West African ancestry with APOL1 risk variants have higher risk of kidney disease. Management: control BP (ACEi/ARB, target < 130/80), glucose, SGLT2 inhibitors to slow progression, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, herbal remedies), adjust drug doses, and treat complications — anaemia (erythropoietin, iron), CKD–mineral bone disorder (phosphate binders, vitamin D), acidosis, and fluid overload. Renal replacement therapy: haemodialysis (costly out-of-pocket in Nigeria — many patients cannot sustain it), peritoneal dialysis and kidney transplantation (living donor transplants performed in several Nigerian centres).

topics.title: Liver Disease
topics.summary: Hepatitis, cirrhosis and complications, hepatocellular carcinoma and liver function tests.

material.heading: Liver tests and hepatitis
material.body: Liver function tests: ALT and AST (hepatocellular injury — very high in viral or drug hepatitis; AST:ALT > 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease), ALP and GGT (cholestasis), bilirubin, and synthetic function — albumin and prothrombin time/INR (best acute marker of liver function). Jaundice is pre-hepatic (haemolysis — unconjugated), hepatic, or post-hepatic/obstructive (pale stools, dark urine, pruritus). Chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg > 6 months) is the leading cause of chronic liver disease in Nigeria; treat with tenofovir or entecavir if active disease, cirrhosis or high viral load. Drug-induced liver injury (anti-TB drugs, paracetamol overdose, herbal remedies) and alcohol are other causes. Acute liver failure: jaundice, coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) and encephalopathy within weeks of onset in a previously normal liver.
keyPoints: Obstructive jaundice: pale stools, dark urine

material.heading: Cirrhosis and HCC
material.body: Cirrhosis (fibrosis with regenerative nodules) results from chronic hepatitis B and C, alcohol, NAFLD/MASLD and others. Complications of portal hypertension and liver failure: ascites (diuretics — spironolactone ± furosemide, salt restriction, paracentesis with albumin; spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — ascitic neutrophils > 250/mm³, treat with cefotaxime), variceal bleeding (resuscitate, terlipressin or octreotide, antibiotics, endoscopic band ligation; prevent with non-selective beta-blockers), hepatic encephalopathy (lactulose, rifaximin; precipitants — bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives, electrolyte disturbance), hepatorenal syndrome and coagulopathy. Severity by Child–Pugh score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) and MELD. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is among the commonest cancers in Nigerian men, linked to hepatitis B, aflatoxin exposure (mouldy stored grains and groundnuts) and cirrhosis; presents with RUQ mass, weight loss and raised alpha-fetoprotein, often at an advanced stage. Surveillance with ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months in high-risk patients; HBV vaccination is the key prevention.

topics.title: Gastrointestinal Disorders
topics.summary: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, diarrhoeal diseases, typhoid and GI cancers.

material.heading: Upper GI
material.body: Dyspepsia is common; Helicobacter pylori infection is highly prevalent in Nigeria and causes gastritis, peptic ulcers and gastric cancer. Test with urea breath test or stool antigen (stop PPIs 2 weeks before). Eradication: triple therapy for 14 days (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole). NSAIDs (including over-the-counter use) are the other major cause of ulcers. Alarm features needing endoscopy: age > 55 with new symptoms, weight loss, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding and anaemia. Upper GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena): causes — peptic ulcer (commonest), varices, gastritis, Mallory–Weiss tear, cancer. Management: ABC, large-bore IV access, blood transfusion (restrictive threshold Hb < 7–8 g/dL except in varices/cardiac disease), risk scoring (Glasgow–Blatchford), IV PPI after endoscopy for ulcers, and urgent endoscopy within 24 hours.
keyPoints: H. pylori: ulcers and gastric cancer

material.heading: Lower GI and infections
material.body: Acute diarrhoea is mostly infectious (viral, bacterial — E. coli, Shigella (bloody dysentery), Campylobacter, cholera — profuse rice-water stools, parasitic — amoebiasis, Giardia); the key is rehydration (ORS; IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration). Antibiotics for dysentery (ciprofloxacin/azithromycin), cholera (doxycycline or azithromycin — reduce duration) and amoebiasis (metronidazole). Typhoid (enteric) fever (Salmonella Typhi): step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly; diagnosis by blood culture (the Widal test is unreliable and over-used); complications include intestinal perforation (terminal ileum) and GI bleeding; treat with ceftriaxone or azithromycin given rising fluoroquinolone resistance. Chronic diarrhoea in HIV (Cryptosporidium, Isospora — acid-fast stains). Inflammatory bowel disease is increasingly recognised. Colorectal cancer incidence is rising in Nigeria, often presenting young and late — rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia need colonoscopy.
